paragraphs: AdaNet treats the design of a neural network as part of the learning problem. Its framework learns both the network’s structure and its weights, adapting them together. These are two different kinds of decisions: structure determines the organization of the network, while weights determine how that organization processes information. Learning both lets the architecture respond to the problem being learned.

The central contribution is a theoretical framework that supports this adaptive process. The paper provides learning guarantees that depend on the data, connecting the resulting architecture to the complexity of the particular problem. Architecture adaptation is therefore accompanied by a formal justification, rather than being presented only as a design choice that might work empirically.

The stated result is that the final architecture provably adapts to problem complexity within this framework. This matters because choosing a network structure and fitting its parameters are closely related decisions. AdaNet brings those decisions into a common learning methodology, with data-dependent guarantees supporting their joint adaptation.
icml-2017-adanet-adaptive-structural-lea.tldr: AdaNet jointly learns neural network structure and weights, with data-dependent guarantees that its architecture adapts to problem complexity.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to replace a matrix with a simpler, low-rank matrix while controlling the errors in its individual entries. It measures those errors using an entrywise ℓp objective, allowing any p of at least one. The familiar singular value decomposition problem appears as the special case p = 2, placing the work within a broader family of approximation problems.

The authors provide approximation algorithms with provable quality guarantees across this entire range of p. Their stated novelty is obtaining the first such algorithms that work for every value in the specified range. The guarantee concerns how well the algorithms approximate the objective; the abstract does not claim that they always find an exact optimum.

The algorithms also expose tradeoffs among approximation quality, computation time, and the rank of the matrix they produce. These competing quantities make the contribution more than a single accuracy result: they describe different ways to balance simplicity and computational effort. The authors report that the methods are straightforward to implement and perform well in practice.
icml-2017-algorithms-for-ell-p-low-rank-.tldr: The paper gives provably good low-rank approximation algorithms for every entrywise ℓp objective with p ≥ 1, exposing tradeoffs in quality, runtime, and rank.

paragraphs: This paper extends a hierarchical Dirichlet process hidden Markov model so that prior knowledge about similarity between states can influence transitions. The desired behavior is that movement between nearby states should be more likely. Here, nearby is defined by a similarity function on the state space, rather than necessarily referring to physical distance.

The model scales transition probabilities using similarities between pairs of states. This creates relationships among transition distributions, but learning the model requires a suitable inference method. The authors introduce an augmented representation as a Markov jump process in which attempted transitions can fail. The probability that an attempt succeeds is proportional to the similarity of its source and destination.

That representation restores conditional conjugacy, providing a mathematical structure that permits a simple Gibbs sampler. Thus, the work contributes both a way to express similarity-based transition preferences and a practical route to inference. Evaluations on speaker diarization, harmonic parsing of four-part chorales, and synthetic datasets show favorable comparisons with existing models.
icml-2017-an-infinite-hidden-markov-mode.tldr: The model favors transitions between similar hidden states and uses an augmented jump-process representation to enable simple Gibbs sampling.

paragraphs: Binary classifiers are often judged using measures that summarize predictions collectively. The F-measure and Jaccard measure are examples: they cannot be expressed as a simple average of separate scores for individual examples. This non-decomposability makes theoretical analysis difficult, because the evaluation objective does not split into independent contributions in the usual way.

The paper examines two distinct settings and corresponding notions of consistency that have arisen around these metrics. It studies both from statistical and algorithmic perspectives. The purpose is to establish how the settings connect and where they differ, so that conclusions about learning behavior are interpreted within the setting to which they actually apply.

The contribution is a comparative theoretical analysis across a broad range of metrics. It complements earlier results and clarifies confusions surrounding the two settings. Its practical significance is guidance for reasoning about binary classification when the evaluation measure has a collective structure: choosing a metric also requires care about what kind of consistency is being analyzed.
icml-2017-consistency-analysis-for-binar.tldr: The paper clarifies two settings for consistency in binary classification with non-decomposable metrics, explaining their statistical and algorithmic connections and differences.

paragraphs: Learning deep models with discrete hidden variables presents two linked challenges: computing useful gradients and choosing update sizes that suit different hidden factors and layers. This paper addresses those difficulties for the Poisson gamma belief network. It derives an alternative representation of that model, called deep latent Dirichlet allocation, that supports a new inference procedure.

The authors use data augmentation and marginalization to derive a block-diagonal Fisher information matrix and its inverse. These quantities describe the geometry relevant to updating the model’s global parameters, which are constrained to lie on a simplex. The block structure supplies a tractable basis for incorporating that geometry into stochastic gradient sampling.

The resulting method, TLASGR MCMC, jointly learns global parameters across all topics and layers while assigning topic-specific and layer-specific learning rates. The approach therefore addresses adaptation of update sizes as an explicit part of inference. The authors report state-of-the-art results on large datasets, supporting the usefulness of this combination of model reformulation and adaptive sampling.
icml-2017-deep-latent-dirichlet-allocati.tldr: A reformulation of the Poisson gamma belief network enables geometry-aware stochastic inference with learning rates adapted to individual topics and layers.

paragraphs: The paper targets optimization problems where evaluating a proposed input is costly and the objective function is treated as a black box. Its algorithm, DB-GP-UCB, selects a batch of inputs jointly. This allows the selection process to consider the batch together while retaining scalability as the number of inputs in the batch grows.

To achieve this, the authors extend Gaussian process upper confidence bound optimization to a batch formulation that admits a Markov approximation. They then express the approximated problem as a distributed constraint optimization task involving multiple agents. This formulation lets them use efficient solvers to obtain computation time that grows linearly with batch size.

The Markov order provides a control over the balance between approximation quality and computational efficiency. The paper also supplies cumulative regret bounds that give a theoretical guarantee on convergence rate. Experiments on synthetic benchmark functions and a real-world optimization problem show better performance than existing batch Bayesian optimization algorithms, supporting the approach in the evaluated settings.
icml-2017-distributed-batch-gaussian-pro.tldr: DB-GP-UCB jointly selects optimization batches through a distributed Markov approximation, balancing computational efficiency with approximation quality and providing regret guarantees.

paragraphs: In a linear structural equation model, identification asks whether causal parameters can be uniquely determined from an observational covariance matrix. Observational relationships alone do not automatically settle that question. The paper develops an approach based on auxiliary variables that generalizes instrumental-variable methods, expanding the tools available for determining which causal coefficients can be recovered.

The main algorithm builds on a new graph-based characterization of conditional independence relationships between auxiliary variables and variables already in the model. These relationships support identification decisions. The authors show that the algorithm subsumes previous leading methods: it identifies all the cases those methods cover and also identifies additional coefficients and models.

The same characterization can incorporate limited experimental information or new substantive knowledge about the domain, allowing identification in additional circumstances. The paper also develops an auxiliary-variable procedure for model testing. Together, these contributions use the auxiliary-variable framework both to recover causal parameters when identification is possible and to examine the proposed structural model.
icml-2017-identification-and-model-testi.tldr: Auxiliary variables extend instrumental-variable methods to identify more linear causal models and support model testing and incorporation of additional knowledge.

paragraphs: The paper develops a neural encoder-decoder that turns an image into markup describing its presentation. It evaluates the approach on mathematical expressions, where the target is LaTeX. The authors also introduce a dataset pairing real-world rendered expressions with their LaTeX markup, providing examples that directly connect visual mathematical content with its textual representation.

Attention is central to handling this non-standard recognition task. The authors show that attention-based approaches can tackle it, unlike the CTC-based neural OCR techniques considered. To reduce the computational cost of attention during inference, they introduce a coarse-to-fine layer. It first selects a support region and then applies attention within that selected region.

The approach substantially outperforms classical mathematical OCR systems on rendered data from the evaluation domain. With pretraining, it also performs well on handwritten data outside that domain. These findings support attention-based image-to-markup generation, while the regional selection mechanism addresses its inference cost. The handwritten result is specifically tied to the use of pretraining.
icml-2017-image-to-markup-generation-wit.tldr: An attention-based encoder-decoder converts mathematical images to LaTeX, using coarse-to-fine region selection to reduce inference complexity.

paragraphs: Continuous-control systems must often choose actions within physical bounds. The paper identifies a problem with using the standard Gaussian distribution as a stochastic policy in this setting: the bounded action space introduces bias. This makes the policy’s distributional form relevant to learning, beyond the choice of neural network or reinforcement learning algorithm.

The authors propose a Beta-distribution policy as an alternative and analyze the bias and variance of policy gradients for both distributions. They show that the Beta policy avoids the bias at issue. The contribution links the choice of action distribution to the statistical behavior of the gradient used to improve the policy.

The paper evaluates both policies with trust region policy optimization and actor critic with experience replay, covering the stated on-policy and off-policy methods. In continuous-control environments from OpenAI Gym and MuJoCo, the Beta policy converges significantly faster and earns higher scores than the Gaussian policy. These results support matching the policy distribution to bounded actions in the tested settings.
icml-2017-improving-stochastic-policy-gr.tldr: Beta-distribution policies avoid the bounded-action bias studied in Gaussian policies and improve convergence and scores in the reported continuous-control experiments.

paragraphs: Mobile health applications may need to predict when an event will occur using several kinds of observations, including sensor streams and self-reports. iSurvive addresses this time-to-event problem while emphasizing interpretability. The motivation is that domain scientists should be able to use model parameters and predictions to inform theories and the design of interventions.

The model starts from a continuous time hidden Markov model, which can represent observations arriving at irregular times. Standard versions do not specifically target the time until a future event, and their emission models lack the richness needed for the multimodal setting described. iSurvive extends classical survival analysis to this temporal hidden-state framework.

The paper provides a parameter-learning method for generalized linear model emissions and for fitting the survival component. This combines a representation of changing hidden states with an explicit event-time prediction task. Results on synthetic data and a mobile health drug-use dataset are described as promising, supporting further use of the approach without establishing an intervention outcome.
icml-2017-isurvive-an-interpretable-even.tldr: iSurvive combines survival analysis with a continuous time hidden Markov model to make interpretable event-time predictions from multimodal mobile health data.

paragraphs: This paper explores language modeling with stacked convolutions that use a finite amount of context. The motivation is computational: convolutional processing allows parallelization across tokens in a sequence. The work tests whether this approach can deliver strong language-modeling performance despite using bounded context, including on a benchmark containing long-term dependencies.

The authors introduce a simplified gating mechanism and investigate important architectural choices. They report that the gate outperforms an earlier mechanism considered in the paper. Combined with stacked convolutions, it produces a non-recurrent model whose design supports efficient sequence processing while retaining competitive predictive performance on large language tasks.

The model achieves state-of-the-art results on WikiText-103 and competitive results on Google Billion Words. It also reduces the latency of scoring a sentence by an order of magnitude relative to a recurrent baseline. The authors qualify their historical claim: to their knowledge, this is the first non-recurrent approach competitive with strong recurrent models on these large-scale tasks.
icml-2017-language-modeling-with-gated-c.tldr: Gated convolutional language models achieve strong large-scale benchmark results while reducing sentence-scoring latency through parallelizable finite-context processing.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced labels can be noisy or even adversarial, making it difficult to infer the underlying correct label. This paper focuses on labels with an ordering, such as age, grade, level, or stage. That ordering is a meaningful part of the problem: the possible labels have a structured relationship that an aggregation method can take into account.

The method samples estimated labels from a posterior distribution and introduces a quantity called separating width to assess the quality of those samples among the labeled observations. This supplies an optimization target for aggregation. The proposed algorithm improves that target by solving for multiple linear decision boundaries and adjusting prior distributions.

The authors describe the algorithm as efficient and evaluate it on several real-world datasets, reporting better performance than existing leading methods. The stated findings support this combination of posterior sampling, ordered-label structure, and separating-width optimization. They are empirical comparisons on the evaluated datasets, rather than a claim that the procedure recovers correct labels under every possible pattern of adversarial responses.
icml-2017-learning-to-aggregate-ordinal-.tldr: The method aggregates noisy ordinal labels by sampling candidate labels and optimizing a separating-width objective through decision boundaries and prior adjustments.

paragraphs: The paper addresses multiclass classification when the number of possible labels makes training and prediction expensive. It introduces an online reduction that solves the multiclass problem using binary classification components. Both training time and prediction time grow logarithmically with the number of classes, making the growth in computation much slower than the growth in the label set.

The construction divides the decision into two stages. A tree first selects a small subset of candidate labels with high recall, aiming to retain the relevant label among those candidates. A one-against-some structure then scores the subset with high precision. Candidate selection and final discrimination therefore play complementary roles in the algorithm.

The authors report that combining several simple techniques yields an algorithm superior to earlier logarithmic-time classification approaches while remaining competitive with one-against-all in space. The contribution links computational scaling to a concrete selection-and-scoring design. Its stated benefits cover both the cost of learning and the cost of making predictions.
icml-2017-logarithmic-time-one-against-s.tldr: A tree selects candidate labels and a one-against-some classifier scores them, enabling logarithmic training and prediction time in the number of classes.

paragraphs: Convolution is a major operation in deep neural networks, and its implementation affects both speed and memory use. The paper describes a tension among existing approaches: direct convolution has poor performance, while indirect methods can require substantial extra memory. That overhead can itself reduce performance, making memory consumption part of the computational problem.

MEC addresses this through compact lowering, a way of arranging the input for computation while using much less intermediate memory. After this compact transformation, the method performs several small matrix multiplications in parallel to complete the convolution. The design connects a smaller working representation with a parallel computation strategy.

The reduced memory footprint also improves the efficiency of the memory subsystem, contributing to speed gains. Experiments on both mobile and server platforms show substantial memory reductions and good speedups compared with other indirect convolution algorithms. The stated results indicate that reducing intermediate storage can improve the memory–performance tradeoff for convolution in the evaluated implementations.
icml-2017-mec-memory-efficient-convoluti.tldr: MEC uses compact input lowering and parallel small matrix multiplications to reduce convolution memory overhead and improve speed on mobile and server platforms.

paragraphs: Robust matrix completion seeks to reconstruct a low-rank matrix from a small set of observed entries when some observations may be arbitrarily corrupted. The task combines missing information with unreliable information. This paper proposes a simple iterative method that alternates between a projected gradient descent step and a hard-thresholding step that cleans up some corrupted entries.

The theoretical result addresses both demands of the problem: the method uses a nearly optimal number of observations while tolerating a nearly optimal number of corruptions. The authors also derive a significant improvement over existing runtime bounds for low-rank matrix completion. These results connect efficient computation with recovery from incomplete and corrupted observations.

Applied to robust principal component analysis, which separates a matrix into low-rank and sparse components, the result yields nearly linear runtime in matrix dimensions, compared with quadratic time for the cited leading methods. Empirical results support the theory, and the robust PCA implementation is an order of magnitude faster than existing methods even on moderately sized problems.
icml-2017-nearly-optimal-robust-matrix-c.tldr: Alternating projected gradient descent with hard-thresholding enables nearly optimal robust matrix completion and a nearly linear-time robust PCA algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper studies a stochastic bandit problem with a continuous collection of possible actions. Each action has an expected reward determined by a function that remains fixed but is unknown. The authors introduce two Gaussian process-based strategies, Improved GP-UCB and GP-TS, and analyze the regret accumulated while learning which actions are rewarding.

The regret guarantees rely on a stated relationship between the reward function and the kernel supplied to the algorithms. Specifically, the function must belong to the reproducing kernel Hilbert space associated with that kernel. This assumption connects the mathematical regularity used by the algorithms with the unknown function they are trying to optimize.

The analysis also develops a self-normalized concentration inequality for vector-valued martingales, allowing arbitrary and even infinite dimension. This is a supporting theoretical contribution alongside the two algorithms. Experiments on synthetic and real-world environments show favorable gains over existing strategies in many cases, providing qualified empirical support rather than a claim of improvement in every setting.
icml-2017-on-kernelized-multi-armed-band.tldr: Two Gaussian process bandit algorithms receive regret bounds under an RKHS assumption and show favorable empirical performance in many evaluated settings.

paragraphs: Arithmetic circuits are representations used for tractable probabilistic reasoning. Related representations can impose different combinations of properties, making their capabilities difficult to compare directly. This paper develops a formal basis for such comparisons, aiming to clarify what those properties mean and what computational roles they play.

A central focus is determinism and what changes when that property is relaxed. The authors establish an exponential separation between circuits with and without determinism. They also derive completeness and incompleteness results, using the framework to distinguish capabilities across variants. These results show that seemingly related circuit representations can have substantial formal differences.

The paper additionally examines the computation of most probable explanations, including when this task is tractable and when it is not. Its significance is that tractability must be understood in relation to both a representation’s properties and the inference task being performed. The framework places earlier developments in a common perspective while supporting new results about arithmetic circuits themselves.
icml-2017-on-relaxing-determinism-in-ari.tldr: A formal comparison framework clarifies how arithmetic-circuit properties, especially determinism, affect representational capabilities and the tractability of most probable explanations.

paragraphs: Multiview representation learning seeks latent factors using multiple views of data. Many approaches formulate the task as convex optimization, where appropriate algorithms can reach global optima in polynomial time. The paper is motivated by a gap between this theoretical preference and evidence that heuristic nonconvex methods can also be computationally effective and reach global optima.

The authors study a nonconvex formulation that can be solved efficiently with a simple stochastic gradient descent method. Their main contribution is an analysis of the algorithm’s dynamics using diffusion processes. This provides a way to study the behavior of the stochastic updates and establish a global rate of convergence to global optima for the formulation considered.

Numerical experiments support the theoretical analysis. The significance is a concrete justification for using a simple nonconvex method in this multiview learning problem. The result connects computationally attractive practice with convergence theory for the studied formulation, rather than establishing that arbitrary nonconvex objectives can be optimized globally by stochastic gradient descent.
icml-2017-online-partial-least-square-op.tldr: Diffusion-based analysis establishes a global convergence rate for stochastic gradient descent on a nonconvex multiview representation-learning formulation.

paragraphs: Parseval networks aim to improve the stability of neural network predictions when inputs undergo adversarial perturbations. The design constrains the Lipschitz constants of linear, convolutional, and aggregation layers to be below one. These constants describe sensitivity to changes, so the constraints directly address how layers can amplify differences in their inputs.

The defining weight constraint keeps linear and convolutional weight matrices approximately in the form of Parseval tight frames. These extend the idea of orthogonal matrices to matrices that need not be square. The authors describe an efficient way to maintain the constraints during stochastic gradient descent, connecting the robustness analysis with a usable training procedure.

On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN, the networks match state-of-the-art accuracy while showing greater resistance to adversarial examples than their vanilla counterparts. The authors also report tendencies toward faster training and better use of network capacity. Those additional benefits are qualified tendencies; the main empirical finding pairs competitive accuracy with improved robustness in the reported comparisons.
icml-2017-parseval-networks-improving-ro.tldr: Parseval networks constrain layer sensitivity through approximately Parseval weight matrices, improving adversarial robustness while maintaining strong benchmark accuracy.

paragraphs: Deep Gaussian processes compose multiple Gaussian processes to create flexible probabilistic models. Their appeal combines layered modeling with uncertainty quantification. The paper addresses a practical obstacle to using them: existing inference approaches have limited scalability and can be cumbersome to construct, making the flexibility of the model difficult to exploit at larger scales.

The authors introduce a formulation based on random feature expansions and train it with stochastic variational inference. These are the central ingredients of the proposed learning framework. The reformulation is intended to make inference more practical while preserving the ability to quantify uncertainty accurately, rather than treating uncertainty as separate from the model’s predictive role.

The evaluation covers several datasets with as many as eight million observations and model architectures with up to thirty hidden layers. The authors report substantial progress over existing deep Gaussian process inference methods in scalability and performance. These demonstrations establish the scale and architectural depth explored in the paper, alongside its stated uncertainty-quantification benefits.
icml-2017-random-feature-expansions-for-.tldr: Random feature expansions and stochastic variational inference make deep Gaussian processes more scalable while retaining accurate uncertainty quantification.

paragraphs: RobustFill compares two approaches to learning behavior from input/output examples. Neural program synthesis produces an explicit program, while neural program induction directly produces outputs using an internal program representation. The paper compares both on a large-scale real-world task and also evaluates rule-based synthesis, whose program generation relies on hand-crafted semantics.

The neural models use a modified attention recurrent network to encode sets containing varying numbers of input/output pairs. They achieve 92% accuracy on the real-world test set, compared with 34% for the previous best neural synthesis approach. The synthesis model also outperforms a comparable induction model on the task, but the authors emphasize that relative strengths depend strongly on the evaluation metric and intended application.

The paper further shows that training can make the neural models robust to realistic input/output noise, including typos. In the noise setting reported, a highly engineered rule-based system fails entirely. Together, the comparisons highlight both improved neural performance and the importance of choosing a program-learning approach around the user’s task and evaluation criteria.
icml-2017-robustfill-neural-program-lear.tldr: RobustFill improves neural learning from input/output examples and handles realistic noise, while showing that synthesis-versus-induction advantages depend on the application and metric.

paragraphs: Time series can describe similar behavior while differing in length or in when particular changes occur. Dynamic time warping addresses this by finding a low-cost alignment between sequences, accommodating shifts and stretching along the time axis. This paper develops soft-DTW, a smoothed version suitable for use as a differentiable learning loss.

Soft-DTW replaces the minimum alignment cost with a soft minimum over all alignment costs. The authors show that both its value and its gradient can be computed in quadratic time and space. The space requirement is a stated computational tradeoff: ordinary DTW takes quadratic time but can use linear space.

The paper demonstrates that this smoothing works particularly well for averaging and clustering time series according to DTW geometry, substantially outperforming the existing baselines considered. It also proposes training a model that outputs time series by minimizing soft-DTW against target sequences. The contribution makes alignment-sensitive comparison directly usable in gradient-based learning, while retaining explicit computational costs.
icml-2017-soft-dtw-a-differentiable-loss.tldr: Soft-DTW smooths time-series alignment into a differentiable loss, improving the reported averaging and clustering results and enabling gradient-based sequence fitting.

paragraphs: Binary hashing supports fast search in large databases by representing items with compact binary codes. Learning these codes is difficult because the hash function must produce discrete outputs. The paper also questions the largely heuristic objectives used by existing methods and proposes a generative approach with a compression-based learning principle.

The method uses the Minimum Description Length principle to learn codes intended to compress the dataset maximally. An associated generative model can use those codes to regenerate inputs. This links the hash representation to information needed to describe and reconstruct the data, providing a common objective for the hash function and the generative model.

The authors develop an efficient algorithm based on stochastic distributional gradients to jointly optimize both sets of parameters while addressing the difficulty caused by binary outputs. Experiments across several large-scale datasets show better retrieval results than existing leading methods. The findings support the proposed combination of a compression-based objective, generative modeling, and a learning procedure designed for discrete codes.
icml-2017-stochastic-generative-hashing-.tldr: Stochastic Generative Hashing jointly learns binary codes and a generative model through a compression objective, improving retrieval in large-scale experiments.

paragraphs: Covariance estimation describes how components of data vary together, but large, high-dimensional datasets can make it expensive to communicate, store, and process the observations. This paper estimates covariance from compressed data. Its central design choice is to make compression depend on the data through weighted sampling, instead of using a data-oblivious compression scheme.

The authors prove that their estimator is unbiased, meaning that averaging over the sampling randomness recovers the quantity being estimated. They also show that specially designed sampling distributions allow the method to achieve the same accuracy with less data. That second benefit is tied to the sampling distributions used, rather than being asserted for every possible weighted sampling scheme.

The paper describes efficient computational procedures and reports experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets that substantially outperform existing leading algorithms. The combined theoretical and empirical results support an improved balance between estimation accuracy and computational cost. The approach makes the design of the compressed representation an active part of accurate covariance estimation.
icml-2017-toward-efficient-and-accurate-.tldr: Data-aware weighted sampling enables unbiased covariance estimation from compressed data, with designed sampling distributions reducing the data needed for a given accuracy.

paragraphs: Synthetic gradients let a neural network layer update without waiting for the true error gradient to arrive through backpropagation. This supports decoupled neural interfaces, where parts of a network can learn asynchronously using local information. The paper investigates what this changes about feed-forward networks’ representational abilities, optimization behavior, and learned internal representations.

The authors show that incorporating synthetic gradients does not alter the learning system’s representational strength. They also prove convergence for linear and deep linear models. These are distinct findings: preserving what a network can represent does not by itself establish how training behaves, so the convergence analysis supplies an additional result for those specified model classes.

On practical problems, the paper examines how synthetic-gradient estimators approximate the true loss and how this can produce drastically different representations across layers. Thus, unchanged representational capacity can coexist with substantial changes in what individual layers learn. The authors also connect synthetic gradients with other error-approximation methods, providing shared language for comparing their mechanisms.
icml-2017-understanding-synthetic-gradie.tldr: Synthetic gradients preserve representational strength and have convergence guarantees for linear models, while potentially producing markedly different learned layer representations.
